steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on translating natural language into temporal logic using large language models. Cover why temporal logic matters and why an NL-to-TL model is needed, what current approaches lack, our approach (LLM-assisted dataset creation, finetuning, lifted NL/TL), our contributions, and a short note on a comparison with GPT-4.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Temporal logic as a precise specification language
- Why translate NL to TL
- Missing requirements in current NL-to-TL tools
- Data bottleneck
- Our approach: pre-trained LLMs and lifted NL/TL
- Contributions
- Ad-hoc comparison with GPT-4

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Temporal Logic (TL)
  - mathematically precise requirement language; robotics (cite), electronics design (cite), autonomous driving (cite)
  - captures spatial, temporal, logical requirements of human language + environmental constraints
  - transformable into executable actions / control inputs for robots (cite)
- Why NL-to-TL
  - many robotics works: end-to-end black-box models from natural language (NL) to behaviors (cite)
  - TL as intermediate, twofold benefit: direct planning; identify sources of failure, automatic feedback to non-expert (cite)
  - TL steep learning curve; NL more intuitive for non-experts
  - NL-to-TL model = missing but crucial component for interactive robots, engineering designs
- No general NL-TL translation tool meeting:
  - Cross-domain generalization: training data constrained to single domain; lacking corpus richness; own Atomic Proposition (AP) formats; fail on other domains (cite); TL structure domain-independent
  - Variability of NL instructions: synthetic data built algorithmically, limited NL forms; real utterances not a small rule set; fail on new sentence structures (cite)
- Data bottleneck
  - statistical methods beat rule-based (cite) but need huge datasets
  - expensive, hard to collect; annotator expertise (cite)
  - constraining domain/form relieves data pressure but undermines generalizability (cite)
- Approach
  - pre-trained LLMs: GPT-3 (cite) assists dataset creation; finetune T5 (cite) for NL-to-TL
  - 'lifted' NL and TL for finetuning -> generalizability
  - prior full NL-to-TL: actions -> APs, e.g. "a response is created in Slack" -> "create_Slack"; each work own AP content/style
  - ours: hide all APs during finetuning -> lifted model
  - full NL -> full TL: lifted model + AP recognition, or transfer learning in one domain; compare with/without lifted pre-training
- Contributions
  - cross-domain dataset: 15K lifted pairs via GPT-3-assisted framework, ablations per framework part; 13K collected/cleaned from two domains, lifted; 28K published; new data indispensable across domains
  - lifted NL-to-TL model on T5; beats former state of the art; two methods for full NL-to-STL; vs Seq2Seq and GPT-3 few-shot, five domains; >95% accuracy all domains, <10% domain specific data; Seq2Seq ablation -> T5 capacity essential
- GPT-4 (cite)
  - released near end of this work; ad-hoc few-shot end-to-end test on ChatGPT Plus, 100 samples per domain
  - no GPT-4 API, hourly access limit -> no more samples
  - 77.7% over 300 samples: much lower than ours, higher than GPT-3

steps.text:
Temporal Logic (TL) is widely used as a mathematically precise language for specifying requirements in many engineering domains, like robotics, electronics design, and autonomous driving. TL can capture complex spatial, temporal, and logical requirements of both human languages and environmental constraints, and it can be transformed into executable actions or control inputs for robots.

Many robotics works try to use end-to-end black-box models that infer robotic behaviors directly from natural language (NL). Using structured TL as the intermediate instead has two benefits: the TL can be used directly for planning, and the TL representation can be used to find specific sources of failure and give automatic feedback to a non-expert user. But TL has a steep learning curve, and it is much more intuitive for a non-expert to communicate goals and constraints in NL. So a model that can transform NL instructions into TL is a missing but crucial component for interactive robots and engineering designs.

Right now there is no general tool for automated translation between TL and NL that considers the following requirements:

- Cross-domain generalization. TL is used in many engineering domains, but current NL-to-TL approaches mostly restrict their training data to one domain. These datasets mostly do not have a rich NL-TL corpus, and each one has its own specified format of Atomic Propositions (AP). So the models fail to generalize to other domains, even though the structure of TL itself does not depend on the domain and should be generic.

- Variability of NL instructions. Past work often builds synthetic data algorithmically, which requires limited forms of the NL input. Real-world NL utterances can't be encoded into a small set of rules, and models trained on such homogeneous data fail to generalize to new sentence structures.

- Data bottleneck
  - statistical methods beat rule-based (cite) but need huge datasets
  - expensive, hard to collect; annotator expertise (cite)
  - constraining domain/form relieves data pressure but undermines generalizability (cite)

- Contributions
  - cross-domain dataset: 15K lifted pairs via GPT-3-assisted framework, ablations per framework part; 13K collected/cleaned from two domains, lifted; 28K published; new data indispensable across domains

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Temporal Logic (TL) is widely used as a mathematically precise language for specifying requirements in many engineering domains, like robotics, electronics design, and autonomous driving. TL can capture complex spatial, temporal, and logical requirements of both human languages and environmental constraints, and it can be transformed into executable actions or control inputs for robots.

Many robotics works try to use end-to-end black-box models that infer robotic behaviors directly from natural language (NL). Using structured TL as the intermediate instead has two benefits: the TL can be used directly for planning, and the TL representation can be used to find specific sources of failure and give automatic feedback to a non-expert user. But TL has a steep learning curve, and it is much more intuitive for a non-expert to communicate goals and constraints in NL. So a model that can transform NL instructions into TL is a missing but crucial component for interactive robots and engineering designs.

Right now there is no general tool for automated translation between TL and NL that considers the following requirements:

- Cross-domain generalization. TL is used in many engineering domains, but current NL-to-TL approaches mostly restrict their training data to one domain. These datasets mostly do not have a rich NL-TL corpus, and each one has its own specified format of Atomic Propositions (AP). So the models fail to generalize to other domains, even though the structure of TL itself does not depend on the domain and should be generic.

- Variability of NL instructions. Past work often builds synthetic data algorithmically, which requires limited forms of the NL input. Real-world NL utterances can't be encoded into a small set of rules, and models trained on such homogeneous data fail to generalize to new sentence structures.

A big bottleneck in the NL-to-TL problem is the lack of data. Modern statistical methods can do better than rule-based methods, but they usually need a huge dataset. This data is expensive and hard to collect because the annotators need strong expertise. As said above, restricting the domain or the form of the NL instructions relieves the dataset pressure, but it also unavoidably hurts generalizability.

To help the data creation process and at the same time get around the need for a huge dataset, we propose to use pre-trained LLMs. We use GPT-3 to help create the dataset and we finetune T5 models to specialize in NL-to-TL transformation.

Another part of our approach is that we use ‘lifted’ versions of NL and TL to finetune our model, and this greatly improves generalizability. In previous work, models trained on full NL-to-TL transformation often include converting specific individual actions into APs. For example, the AP "a response is created in Slack" could be formalized as "create_Slack". So every work has to regularize its own content and style of APs, and this affects generalization. We don't do this; instead we hide all the APs in our data during finetuning, and get a lifted model on lifted NL-to-TL transformation. For the final ground application from full NL into full TL we propose two methods, either combining the lifted model with AP recognition, or further transfer learning in one specific domain. For the transfer learning into specific domains, we compare the models with and without pre-training on lifted NL-TL and show that it matters.

We present two key contributions in this paper:

- Building a cross-domain NL-TL dataset. We generate a dataset of 15K lifted NL-TL pairs with a new GPT-3-assisted framework, and we do ablation studies to show why each part of the framework matters for building the dataset. We also collect and clean previous datasets (13K) from two different domains and adapt the original full NL-TL pairs into lifted versions. This way we publish a dataset of 28K lifted NL-TL pairs. The ablation studies show that the newly created data is indispensable, because training only on the collected data does not work across domains.

- Finetuning a lifted NL-to-TL model on T5 with our data and showing the performance improvement over former state-of-the-art methods. For application to full NL-to-STL transformation we propose two methods. We compare our model to Seq2Seq models and to direct few-shot learning with GPT-3, across five domains. The results show that our methods get better accuracy (>95% across all domains) and are more data-efficient (<10% domain specific data). We also do an ablation study where we train a Seq2Seq model with the lifted NL-to-TL dataset, which shows that the superior model capacity of T5 is essential.

GPT-4 came out when we were near the end of this work. To compare the accuracy of direct GPT-4 few-shot end-to-end translation with our finetuned model, we did an ad-hoc test on the ChatGPT Plus version with 100 samples in each domain. We could not test on more samples because we don't have access to the GPT-4 API and the ChatGPT Plus version has an access limit per hour. GPT-4 gets an accuracy of 77.7% over 300 samples, which is much lower than our model but higher than GPT-3.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Temporal Logic (TL) has been widely used as a mathematically precise language to specify requirements in many engineering domains such as robotics [1], electronics design [2], and autonomous driving [3]. TL can capture the complex spatial, temporal, and logical requirements of both human languages and environmental constraints, and can be transformed into executable actions or control inputs for robots [4,5,6,7,8].

Unlike many robotics works that use end-to-end black-box models to infer robotic behaviors directly from natural language (NL) [9], using structured TL as the intermediate has a twofold benefit – the TL can be used for direct planning, and the TL representation can be used to identify specific sources of failure and provide automatic feedback to a non-expert user [5]. However, TL has a steep learning curve, while communicating one’s goals and constraints through NL is much more intuitive to a non-expert. Therefore, a model able to transform NL instructions into TL is a missing but crucial component for interactive robots and engineering designs.

Currently, there is no general tool for automated translation between TL and NL that takes the following requirements into consideration:

- Cross-domain generalization. Although TL is used in many engineering domains, current NL-to-TL approaches largely constrain their training data to a single domain. These datasets mostly lack corpus richness of NL-TL and have their own specified formats of Atomic Propositions (AP). The models then fail to generalize to other domains [8], even though the structure of TL itself does not depend on the domain and should be generic.

- Variability of NL instructions. Past work often constructs synthetic data algorithmically, requiring limited forms of the NL input. Real-world NL utterances cannot be encoded into a small set of rules, and models trained on such homogeneous data fail to generalize to new sentence structures [10].

One big bottleneck in the NL-to-TL problem is the lack of data. Although modern statistical methods can outperform rule-based methods [11], they typically require a huge dataset. This data is expensive and difficult to collect since annotators need strong expertise [10]. As outlined above, constraining the domain or form of the NL instructions relieves the pressure of the dataset, but also unavoidably undermines generalizability [10,12].

To supplement the data creation process and at the same time overcome the need for a huge dataset, we propose to use pre-trained LLMs. We utilize GPT-3 [13] to assist dataset creation and finetune T5 models [14] to specialize in NL-to-TL transformation.

Another aspect of our approach is to use ‘lifted’ versions of NL and TL for finetuning our model, which greatly enhances generalizability. In previous work, models trained on full NL-to-TL transformation often include converting specific individual actions into APs. For example, the AP "a response is created in Slack" might be formalized as "create_Slack". As a result, each work has to regularize its own content and style of APs, which affects generalization. Instead, we hide all the APs in our data during finetuning, acquiring a lifted model on lifted NL-to-TL transformation. For the final ground application from full NL into full TL, we propose two methods: combining the lifted model with AP recognition, or further transfer learning in one specific domain. For transfer learning into specific domains, we compare the models with/without pre-training on lifted NL-TL and show its significance.

In this paper, we present two key contributions:

- Constructing a cross-domain NL-TL dataset. We generate a dataset of 15K lifted NL-TL pairs using a novel GPT-3-assisted framework, and conduct ablation studies to show the significance of each part of the framework for dataset construction. In addition, we collect and clean previous datasets (13K) from two varied domains, adapting the original full NL-TL pairs into lifted versions. In this way, we publish a dataset of 28K lifted NL-TL pairs. Ablation studies show that the newly created data are indispensable, since training purely on the collected data fails to work across domains.

- Finetuning a lifted NL-to-TL model on T5 using our data, and demonstrating improved performance compared to former state-of-the-art methods. For application in full NL-to-STL transformation, we propose two methods. We compare our model to Seq2Seq models and to direct few-shot learning by GPT-3 across five domains. The experimental results show that our methods achieve better accuracy (>95% across all domains) and are more data-efficient (<10% domain specific data). We also do an ablation study by training a Seq2Seq model with the lifted NL-to-TL dataset, which reveals that T5’s superior model capacity is essential.

GPT-4 [15] came out as we were approaching the end of this work. To compare the accuracy of direct GPT-4 few-shot end-to-end translation with our finetuned model, we did an ad-hoc test on the ChatGPT Plus version with 100 samples in each domain. We could not test on more samples since we do not have access to the GPT-4 API and the ChatGPT Plus version has an access limitation per hour. The results show that GPT-4 achieves an accuracy of 77.7% over 300 samples, much lower than our model but higher than GPT-3.
